title: Function-Aware Fill-in-the-Middle as Mid-Training for Coding Agent Foundation Models
hook: Ordinary pretraining only sees code left-to-right. This mid-training trick masks whole functions like a tool call's return value — and it measurably makes coding agents better.
key_points: Notices that a coding agent's tool-call loop (call, get a return value, keep reasoning) mirrors a function call site: caller binds args, callee returns a value, downstream code consumes it.

Trains on function-aware fill-in-the-middle: masking functions chosen via program dependency graph analysis plus a complexity-inferability criterion, on a 2.6B-token decontaminated corpus from 968 GitHub repos.
Mid-training Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct (7B/14B) and Qwen3-8B lifts SWE-Bench-Verified by +2.8 to +3.2 points and SWE-Bench-Lite by +3.7 to +5.4 points, before any agentic post-training.
Gains hold across two different agentic post-training pipelines (R2E-Gym, SWE-Smith) and a non-Qwen2.5 base model.

Also mitigates the capability erosion that agentic post-training normally causes on non-agent coding (LiveCodeBench) and non-coding tool-use benchmarks (tau-bench, BFCL) — despite the corpus being Python-only.
content_html: Standard code pretraining reads left to right — but a coding agent's real job is different: call a tool, get back a result computed somewhere else, and keep reasoning from there. This paper's insight is that this loop already has a natural analogue buried in ordinary code: a function call, where a caller hands off arguments and later consumes a return value it didn't compute itself.
extra_html:
Yubo Wang and colleagues turn that analogy into a self-supervised mid-training objective: function-aware fill-in-the-middle, which masks out functions selected via program dependency graph analysis and a complexity-inferability criterion, then trains the model to fill them back in. Applied to Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct (7B and 14B) and Qwen3-8B on a 2.6-billion-token decontaminated corpus from 968 GitHub repositories, it lifts SWE-Bench-Verified by 2.8-3.2 points and SWE-Bench-Lite by 3.7-5.4 points — and those gains survive two different downstream agentic post-training pipelines (R2E-Gym, SWE-Smith) and a different base model.

The more surprising result: agentic post-training usually erodes a model's non-agentic coding skill (on benchmarks like LiveCodeBench) and general tool-use ability (tau-bench, BFCL), but models that went through this mid-training step hold onto those capabilities better — even though the mid-training corpus is exclusively Python. The authors read this as evidence that the function-call inductive bias, once learned, survives later training stages. Wang and colleagues, arXiv 2026.

related.title: Qwen3-Coder
related.hook: Qwen3-Coder is an open-weight agentic coding model — a 480B Mixture-of-Experts built for long-horizon, tool-using software tasks, rivaling closed models on agentic coding.

related.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real GitHub Issues?
related.hook: Test a coding agent on real GitHub issues with real test suites - not toy problems - and the bar turns out to be much harder than HumanEval suggested.

flashcards.prompt: What structural similarity motivates function-aware fill-in-the-middle as mid-training for coding agents?
flashcards.back_html: A coding agent's action-observation-continuation loop is structurally like a function call site: a caller binds arguments, a callee returns a value computed elsewhere, and downstream code consumes it — a pattern that's already everywhere in ordinary code.

flashcards.prompt: How does this mid-training method pick which functions to mask?

choices.text: Via program dependency graph analysis combined with a complexity-inferability double criterion
By masking every function in the corpus at random
By masking only the shortest functions in each file

flashcards.explanation_html: The selection criterion targets functions that are both structurally meaningful (via dependency graph analysis) and plausible to infer, rather than masking arbitrarily.

flashcards.prompt: What happens to non-agent and non-coding capabilities after mid-training plus agentic post-training, compared to skipping mid-training?
flashcards.back_html: Normally agentic post-training erodes non-agent coding (LiveCodeBench) and non-coding tool-use (tau-bench, BFCL) skills; adding this mid-training step mitigates that erosion, even though its corpus is Python-only.

flashcards.prompt: Does the SWE-Bench improvement from mid-training depend on a specific agentic post-training pipeline?

choices.text: No — the gains hold across two different pipelines (R2E-Gym and SWE-Smith) and a non-Qwen2.5 base model
Yes, it only worked with one specific post-training pipeline
The paper only tested one post-training pipeline, so this is unknown

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors explicitly test two agentic post-training pipelines plus a different base model (Qwen3-8B with SWE-Lego) and see the improvement hold in each case.
